title: The Architect's Son: Vienna, Babelsberg, the Ministry, and the Long American Exile
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Vienna, and the Years He Later Rewrote

stops.name: Vienna, Schenkenstrasse 6: the birth
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested. The address comes from the baptismal register as cited by German Wikipedia, corroborated by the baptism at the Schottenkirche a few hundred metres up the same street; Lang himself named a different address, near the Stephansdom. An earlier reading of this dossier placed the family in Mariahilf at 48.1975, 16.3542, about two kilometres southwest, with no source support; that pin is withdrawn.
stops.campa: Friedrich Christian Anton Lang is born on the fifth of December in a first-district apartment house on the Schenkenstrasse, second son of the architect Anton Lang and of Pauline Schlesinger, born Jewish and received into the Catholic church before the birth. On the twenty-eighth he is carried up the street to the Schottenkirche on the Freyung and baptized. From 1895 his mother runs the building firm A. Lang und Cie. The son will spend his life telling interviewers that he grew up in the shadow of the Stephansdom, and that his mother kept house.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, in Fritz Lang: Interviews (University Press of Mississippi), as cited in the Wikipedia article on Lang
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the Schottenkirche, Vienna, entry of 28 December 1890
The house at Schenkenstrasse 6, Innere Stadt
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Fritz Lang' (baptismal register; A. Lang und Cie)
Patrick McGilligan, Fritz Lang: The Nature of the Beast (1997)

stops.name: Vienna, the city of the fathers
stops.date_confidence: Period marker, not a dated event; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin is the corpus coordinate for Vienna, shared byte for byte with Freud's journey.
stops.campa: The Vienna of his boyhood is the city Sigmund Freud is then taking apart from a consulting room on the Berggasse, a capital where every life keeps two accounts, the one given at table and the one underneath. Lang's accounts will run the same way. The architect wants an architect; the boy fills sketchbooks with faces and drifts toward the cafe crowd of would-be painters. Both men will get out ahead of the same regime, Lang from Berlin in 1933, Freud through Paris in 1938.
stops.quote: if you do not teach religion, how can you teach ethics?
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, cited in Mark Kermode, Hatchet Job, as reproduced in the Wikipedia article on Lang
suggested_refs: Freud's consulting room at Berggasse 19, contemporary with Lang's Viennese boyhood
sources: McGilligan, Fritz Lang: The Nature of the Beast (1997)

stops.name: Vienna, the Technische Hochschule: one semester
stops.date_confidence: Enrolment protocol cited by German Wikipedia: matriculated in the winter semester 1909/10, withdrawn after a single semester. English Wikipedia's 1908, and the reading of a sustained 1908 to 1910 course in civil engineering, are not supported by that protocol. The two lenses of this dossier disagreed; the protocol is followed and the disagreement is left on the record.
stops.campa: At the Technische Hochschule on the Karlsplatz he matriculates in his father's trade, entered in the enrolment protocol for the winter semester. He leaves after one term. For the rest of his life the interviews will describe a course in engineering and architecture abandoned for art, a young manhood of study given up in a single gesture. The register holds one semester and a withdrawal. The story makes better cinema than the register does, and he keeps it in circulation for sixty years.
suggested_refs: The enrolment protocol of the Technische Hochschule Wien, winter semester 1909/10

stops.name: Vienna, the Academy of Fine Arts: the refusal
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates the rejection to 1910/11 and the eventual admission to 1918; no month is given for either, so both default to 01. The pin is the Academy building on the Schillerplatz.
stops.campa: He applies to the Academy of Fine Arts on the Schillerplatz and is turned down. He is admitted only in 1918, home from the war with one eye. The refusal appears in nothing he ever tells about himself. In its place he puts the wandering years, and they run to caravans. German Wikipedia takes both dates from the Academy's own files. Two entries in a register, eight years apart: the first he buries for life, the second he never bothers to mention either, because by 1918 the scenarios are already selling in Berlin.
suggested_refs: The Akademie der bildenden Kuenste, Schillerplatz, and its admission files for 1910 and 1918

stops.name: Munich, Schwabing: the wandering years
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The Schwabing rooms and the whole grand tour Lang described later, given by English Wikipedia as Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific, rest on his own interviews. McGilligan finds the itinerary largely unsupported by documents and treats it as self-mythology. The 1911 date is a placeholder inside a range Lang himself gave as roughly 1910 to 1913.
stops.campa: By his own account he leaves Vienna and goes wandering. Munich first, the painters' quarter of Schwabing, caricatures and postcards sold for bread; then Europe, then Africa, then Asia and the Pacific, an itinerary that grows and shifts across sixty years of interviews and never quite settles into one route. McGilligan, working through what paper exists, finds almost none of it documented. The wandering years are the first film Lang directs, with himself in the part, and the Schwabing rooms are the likeliest true thing in them.
suggested_refs: McGilligan's chapter on the pre-war years, weighing Lang's travel accounts against the documentary record

stops.name: Paris, Montmartre: the painter
stops.date_confidence: The fact of a Paris sojourn before August 1914 is broadly accepted (Eisner 1976); the year comes from Lang and the month is defaulted to 01. McGilligan holds the texture of the account unreliable, and this dossier flags the whole pre-war stretch as contested.
stops.campa: He settles on the butte at Montmartre to paint and to sell what he paints. Eisner takes the year from Lang; McGilligan doubts the colouring and not the fact. It is the last ordinary year of the old Europe, and he spends it at an easel among other men at easels, an Austrian subject living in a French city fourteen months before the two governments turn that from a detail into a condition. He is twenty-two and, on every account including his own, has not yet seen a film he wanted to make.
suggested_refs: The Montmartre studios and dealers of 1913, Lang's stated Paris milieu

stops.name: Paris, the enemy alien
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; the day of the arrest is not given in reachable sources and is defaulted to the opening of the war. The escape is known only from Lang's own account. The pin is the corpus coordinate for Paris.
stops.campa: War is declared and the painter becomes a category. French authorities arrest him as a subject of Austria-Hungary, one of thousands of foreigners swept up in the first days. He gets out and makes his way back to Vienna. He will tell the escape a number of ways over the years, and the ways do not agree; what is not in doubt is that a man who left Vienna to stop being his father's son is returned to Vienna by a police order, in the first month of a war that will take four years and his right eye.
suggested_refs: French internment of enemy aliens, August 1914

stops.name: Vienna, the muster roll
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia, citing the muster record: called for Landsturm service in November 1914, conscripted in January 1915 as an Einjaehrig-Freiwilliger, a one-year service category and not an act of volunteering. English Wikipedia says drafted. The claim that Lang volunteered comes from Lang, and the chronology lens of this dossier repeated it; it is not followed here.
stops.campa: The muster record has him called for Landsturm service in November and conscripted in January, in the one-year service category whose German name contains the word volunteer and whose substance does not. Lang will later say he enlisted. It is a small correction and a characteristic one: in every version he tells, the thing that happens to him is converted into a thing he chose. The army does not care either way. It gives him a uniform and sends him east.
suggested_refs: The Austro-Hungarian muster record for Lang, November 1914 and January 1915

stops.name: Galicia, the Russian front
stops.date_confidence: Service against Russia runs 1915 into 1916; the documented wound is dated 17 June 1916. Unit positions within Galicia are not specified in reachable sources, and the pin marks Lemberg as a regional anchor rather than a site. An earlier range beginning in 1914 is corrected by the muster record. The month here is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He serves in Galicia against the Russians, in the theatre that eats the Austro-Hungarian army by the hundred thousand. He is wounded more than once; the documented Russian-front wound is dated the seventeenth of June 1916. Shell splinters take the sight of his right eye. The monocle that becomes his signature on every set from Neubabelsberg to Culver City begins here, in a field hospital in the east, as a repair. No source reached names his unit or where in that country it stood.
suggested_refs: Austro-Hungarian casualty records for the Galician front, June 1916
sources: Tom Gunning, The Films of Fritz Lang (2000), citing Lang's Austrian military record

stops.name: The Romanian front
stops.date_confidence: Romania enters the war in August 1916. The month of Lang's deployment and the exact place within the theatre are not specified in reachable sources; the pin marks the centre of the Transylvanian front as a regional anchor.
stops.campa: Romania declares for the Entente in August and a new front opens in the Carpathians. Lang is sent to it, and is wounded again. Between the two theatres he spends the better part of three years being carried out of places on stretchers. What he does with the time in between, on the evidence of what he sells in 1917, is write: the stories that reach Berlin come out of a soldier's notebooks, and the first of them are bought by strangers who have never met him.
suggested_refs: The Transylvanian campaign of autumn 1916

stops.name: Vienna, the hospital bed and the scenarios
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to place: the specific hospital is not named in reachable sources, and the pin marks the Allgemeines Krankenhaus district as the best-supported approximation. Month and day defaulted to 01. The discharge with the rank of lieutenant is attested for 1918.
stops.campa: Convalescing in Vienna, half blind, he writes film scenarios, and the Berlin house of Decla buys several. He also acts a little in Viennese theatre. In 1918 he is discharged with the rank of lieutenant, into a monarchy that has weeks to live. The Academy that refused him at twenty admits him this same year, and he does not stay. Everything he owns fits in a case, his eye is gone, his father's profession is behind him, and a producer in another country has already paid money for his handwriting. He goes where the money is.
suggested_refs: Lang's wartime scenarios purchased by Decla, 1917-1918

segments.name: Decla, Berlin, and the Making of a Style

stops.name: Berlin, the Decla offices
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month approximate. The Decla office address is not confirmed in reachable sources, and the pin marks the Potsdamer Platz film district of the period.
stops.campa: Erich Pommer takes him on at Decla, first as scenario writer and story editor, then, within months, as a director. Berlin in the winter of the revolution is short of coal and long on film companies; the industry that will make the decade is being assembled in rented rooms by men who were soldiers a year ago. Pommer has an eye for what a man can do before the man knows it. He hands the one-eyed Austrian a camera and a schedule, and the schedule is brutal.
suggested_refs: Erich Pommer's Decla-Bioscop, the firm that made Lang a director

stops.name: Berlin-Halensee, the first features
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to place. The 1919 titles are attested; the Halensee working base comes from Gunning (2000) and no address is confirmed. Month approximate.
stops.campa: In one year he directs Halbblut, Der Herr der Liebe, the first part of Die Spinnen, and Harakiri: a melodrama, a romance, a serial adventure, an orientalist tragedy. He is learning the whole grammar at commercial speed, in a market that will buy anything with movement in it. Within two years he is a director the company can rely on, which in 1920 is worth more to Decla than being a director anyone admires. Die Spinnen runs to a second part the next year, and the crowd that comes for the treasure hunt gets the geometry as well.
suggested_refs: Die Spinnen, part one (1919), Lang's first serial success
sources: Gunning, The Films of Fritz Lang (2000)

stops.name: Charlottenburg, the marriage and the gunshot
stops.date_confidence: Marriage to Elisabeth Rosenthal attested for 13 February 1919 at Charlottenburg; her death by gunshot wound attested for 25 September 1920. The address of the flat is not established in reachable sources, and the pin marks the district of the marriage register. What happened in the room is not established by anything reachable, and this dossier does not decide it.
stops.campa: In February 1919 he marries the theatre actress Elisabeth Rosenthal, called Lisa, in Charlottenburg. In 1920, making the second Spinnen and Das wandernde Bild, he meets the screenwriter Thea von Harbou through the director Joe May. On the twenty-fifth of September Elisabeth dies of a gunshot wound. Lang and von Harbou are charged with failure to render aid; the charge is dropped. No surviving account closes the question. The one account of the room comes from the two people who were charged over it.
suggested_refs: The Berlin police file on the death of Elisabeth Lang, September 1920

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, Der muede Tod
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin is the corpus coordinate for the UFA works at Neubabelsberg, inherited byte for byte from Falconetti's journey; a studio-site reading of 52.3925, 13.0967 appears in the geography notes of this dossier, and the two differ by under a kilometre.
stops.campa: At the Ufa complex in Neubabelsberg he makes Vier um die Frau and then Der muede Tod, three tales of Death outmanoeuvred by a girl who cannot outmanoeuvre him. The lighting and the architecture of the thing travel: Douglas Fairbanks sees it, and by report takes from it what he needs for The Thief of Bagdad. It is the first Lang film that other filmmakers steal from. From here his sets are his argument, and the argument is that fate is built, not felt.
suggested_refs: Der muede Tod (1921), and the effects Fairbanks is said to have taken from it

stops.name: Berlin, the marriage to Thea von Harbou
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to place: the ceremony location within Berlin is not specified in reachable sources, and the pin is the corpus coordinate for Berlin. The date 26 August 1922 comes from McGilligan; the chronology lens gives only the year.
stops.campa: He marries Thea von Harbou. From this year every film he makes in Germany is written by his wife, and the run they write together is the run the century remembers: Dr. Mabuse der Spieler, four hours released in two parts, then Die Nibelungen, then Metropolis, then M. She supplies the myth and the melodrama; he supplies the machine that grinds them. Mabuse is a hypnotist and a financier at once, ruining a city by working on its nerves, and the film runs four hours because the pair of them cannot see where to stop. In eleven years they will divorce over a government, and she will stay.
suggested_refs: Dr. Mabuse der Spieler (1922), the first Lang-Harbou collaboration as married partners

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, Die Nibelungen
stops.date_confidence: Year of release attested; production runs from 1922. Month and day defaulted to 01. Pin as at Der muede Tod.
stops.campa: Two parts, five hours, the national epic staged entirely inside a studio: a forest built out of concrete trunks, a dragon worked by men inside it, Kriemhild's revenge burning down a hall that was never anywhere. Lang refuses location shooting on principle. If the Nibelungenlied happens in a country that does not exist, the film will be shot in a country that does not exist, and Ufa will pay to build it. The dedication is to the German people. Nine years later the government that adopts the dedication offers him the industry.
stops.quote: Jerry, don't forget, the gods have not created men, man has created the gods.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, cited in Tom Gunning, The Films of Fritz Lang: Allegories of Vision and Modernity, as reproduced in the Wikipedia article on Lang
suggested_refs: The constructed forest and hall of Die Nibelungen at Babelsberg, 1922-1924

segments.name: Metropolis, and the Sound That Came After

stops.name: New York, the skyline from the harbour
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 1924 crossing, and the claim that the Manhattan skyline gave him Metropolis, rest on Lang's own accounts as quoted by Minden and Bachmann (2002) and Grant (2003). No independent record of the voyage was reached. The month is a placeholder and the pin marks the Manhattan transatlantic piers.
stops.campa: He crosses to America to see what the Americans do with film, and by his account the city answers before the studios do. He looks at Manhattan from the water at night and calls the buildings a vertical sail, scintillating and very light, a backdrop hung in the dark to dazzle and hypnotize. In the same breath he calls the sight of Neuyork enough on its own to make a film out of. He goes home and builds it out of plaster at Babelsberg, and the machine city keeps the lighting of a harbour at night.
stops.quote: I looked into the streets—the glaring lights and the tall buildings—and there I conceived Metropolis.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, cited in Minden and Bachmann, Fritz Lang's Metropolis: Cinematic Visions of Technology and Fear (2002), p. 4; em dashes as printed
suggested_refs: Lang's 1924 statements on the New York skyline, collected in Grant, Fritz Lang: Interviews (2003)

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, the building of Metropolis
stops.date_confidence: Shooting runs from 1925 into 1926, roughly a year; the month is approximate. Pin as at Der muede Tod.
stops.campa: A year of shooting, thousands of extras, a flooded set, the Schuefftan process working mirrors so that models and actors occupy one frame. The budget goes past anything Ufa has spent and helps push the company into the financial crisis that ends its independence. Lang is thirty-five and has been given a studio to spend as though it were a state. He spends it. Afterwards he disowns the moral of the thing while conceding he is at least half responsible for it, because he is the one who shot it.
stops.quote: The main thesis was Mrs. Von Harbou's, but I am at least 50 percent responsible because I did it...You cannot make a social-conscious picture in which you say that the intermediary between the hand and the brain is the heart.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, interviewed on the authorship of Metropolis, cited in the Wikipedia article on the film
suggested_refs: The Schuefftan process as developed for Metropolis at Babelsberg

stops.name: Berlin, the Ufa-Palast am Zoo: Metropolis opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 10 January 1927.
stops.campa: The premiere is mixed and the accounting is worse; the film loses money and the costs bite into a company already sinking. In the same Berlin, Johannes Itten has been running his own school since 1926, Rudolf Laban moved his Choreographisches Institut into the city in October, and in December John von Neumann will habilitate at the university. The capital is running the same argument about bodies and machines in four buildings at once, and Lang's is the one losing money.
suggested_refs: The Ufa-Palast am Zoo and the reception of Metropolis, January 1927

stops.name: Neubabelsberg, Spione and Frau im Mond
stops.date_confidence: Spione is released in 1928 and Frau im Mond in 1929; the stop covers both productions and the date is set at the start of the run, month and day defaulted to 01. Pin as at Der muede Tod.
stops.campa: Spione, and an affair with its actress Gerda Maurus. Then Frau im Mond, made with the rocket engineer Hermann Oberth advising, which invents the countdown to a launch because a countdown is better drama than a switch. In December 1928 fire takes the original negative of Dreyer's Passion of Joan of Arc at these same Ufa works, where Falconetti's face had been printed and where Lang's machine city was struck. The complex builds the century's images and burns them in the same sheds.
suggested_refs: Hermann Oberth's rocketry consultancy on Frau im Mond, 1928-1929

stops.name: Staaken, the Zeppelin hall: M
stops.date_confidence: Shooting runs from 1930 into 1931; the month is approximate. The pin marks the converted Zeppelin hangar at Staaken used as studio space.
stops.campa: In a converted airship hangar he makes his first sound film: a child-murderer hunted through Berlin by the police and by the underworld at once, until the thieves try him themselves in a cellar. Peter Lorre is unknown when it starts and is not afterwards. The story that Lang threw him down a flight of stairs to get the battered look is repeated everywhere and sourced nowhere. In the same city that November, Wilhelm Reich moves in his practice and joins the Communist Party. Both men are on lists within two years.
suggested_refs: The Staaken Zeppelin hall as film studio, 1930-1931

stops.name: Berlin, Das Testament des Dr. Mabuse
stops.date_confidence: Filming begins in 1932; the month is approximate. The pin is the corpus coordinate for Berlin, not a studio address, which is not established in reachable sources.
stops.campa: The criminal doctor returns, mad in an asylum, dictating a programme for the destruction of the social order through terror while his organisation carries it out. Von Harbou writes it with him, as always. Lang puts the slogans of the ascendant party into the mouths of the gang; he says so afterwards in print, for American audiences, in a statement written when the film has already been forbidden at home. The picture is finished in the last weeks of a republic.
stops.quote: The film was made as an allegory to show Hitler's processes of terrorism. Slogans and doctrines of the Third Reich have been put into the mouths of criminals in the film.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, foreword statement written for the American release of The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, 1933
suggested_refs: Lang's American release statement for The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, 1933
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Testament of Dr. Mabuse'

stops.name: Berlin, the ban
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 30 March 1933. The rationale usually quoted, that the film showed that an extremely dedicated group of people are perfectly capable of overthrowing any state with violence, reaches us through Kalat (2005) and Wikipedia as the reported ground of the decision; it is not a verified verbatim utterance of Goebbels from a primary document, and is presented here as the reported rationale only.
stops.campa: The new regime forbids Das Testament des Dr. Mabuse and cancels the screening. The reason given, as it comes down to us, is not that the film insults the party but that it demonstrates something true: that a small enough and dedicated enough group can bring down any state by violence. The censors have read the picture correctly and banned it for being right. Lang has made a film about terror as a method, in the month the method takes the country.
suggested_refs: The censorship decision of 30 March 1933 against Das Testament des Dr. Mabuse
sources: David Kalat, The Strange Case of Dr. Mabuse (2005), as cited there
English Wikipedia, 'The Testament of Dr. Mabuse'

stops.name: Berlin, Wilhelmstrasse 49: the Propaganda Ministry
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The meeting is not seriously disputed, but nothing contemporary fixes it: Goebbels' diary does not mention it, no date is documented, and the scene comes entirely from Lang's own retellings from the 1940s onward, which McGilligan shows grew in successive tellings. Tagging the summons as attested while tagging the flight that follows from it as legend was inconsistent, and is corrected. Month follows Lang's placement of it just after the ban.
stops.campa: By his own telling he is summoned to Wilhelmstrasse 49 and finds the minister who banned him full of praise: Metropolis, M, here is the man to run German film. From the same ministry, in 1934, Goebbels will set Rudolf Laban over the Deutsche Tanzbuehne, and in December of that year Mary Wigman will dance at the festival mounted under the Reich Culture Chamber. The offer Lang refuses is the harness the dancers accept, from the same man, in the same corridor, within eighteen months.
suggested_refs: The Reichsministerium fuer Volksaufklaerung und Propaganda, Wilhelmstrasse 49

stops.name: Berlin, Anhalter Bahnhof: the night train that may not have run
stops.date_confidence: The permanent departure is dated 31 July 1933 in the chronology. Lang's own story places a single overnight flight immediately after the Goebbels meeting: jewelry sold, bank left behind, one train. The passport shows he did not leave until June and travelled repeatedly between France and Germany through 1933, and that he changed money at his bank; German Wikipedia has him shuttling between Berlin, London and Paris for about three months. The contradiction is left standing. Wikipedia attaches the passport finding to Kracauer (1947), which cannot support it; the research is Goesta Werner (1990) and McGilligan (1997).
stops.campa: In the version he tells for forty years there is one night: he sells his wife's jewelry, takes the evening train, and is over the border before the ministry can want an answer. In the version the passport keeps there are months of crossings, a bank counter, London, Paris, Berlin again, and a departure at the end of July. Both are now in the canon and neither has dislodged the other. The man who built fate out of girders spends the rest of his life editing the one story he could not shoot twice.
stops.quote: Goebbels' diary makes no mention of such a meeting and Lang's passport also shows that he did not leave until June and made repeated trips between France and Germany throughout 1933.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'The Testament of Dr. Mabuse', Release section, verbatim; the reference attached there to Kracauer 1947 is misapplied, the finding being Werner 1990 and McGilligan 1997
suggested_refs: Lang's 1933 passport, examined by Goesta Werner (1990) and by McGilligan (1997)
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Testament of Dr. Mabuse'

stops.name: Paris, the exile's year
stops.date_confidence: The Paris period runs 1933 to 1934; the month is approximate. Lang's address in the city is not established in reachable sources, and the pin is the corpus coordinate for Paris. The divorce from von Harbou is attested for 1933 without a date.
stops.campa: He spends about a year in Paris among the French film people, and the marriage ends: Thea von Harbou stays in Germany and joins the party, and the writing partnership that made every German film he signed is over by decree of the two of them. Paris is the first station for everyone leaving the Reich. Laban will pass through it in 1937 on his way to England, Freud in June 1938 on his way to London. The city is a waiting room with a good address, and the German film trade sets up its offices there for a season before the whole of it moves again, west, on studio money.
suggested_refs: The German film emigration in Paris, 1933-1934

stops.name: Joinville-le-Pont, the Joinville studios: Liliom
stops.date_confidence: Liliom is shot in 1934 at the Joinville studios southeast of Paris, where Erich Pommer's Fox-Europa was based after moving to France in April 1933. An earlier reading of this dossier placed the shoot at Epinay-sur-Seine, 48.9550, 2.3106, about seventeen kilometres north; that is corrected. The month is approximate.
stops.campa: His only French film, and Pommer produces it, as Pommer produced the first ones in Berlin: Molnar's play about a fairground barker who dies badly and is put on trial in heaven, with Charles Boyer and Madeleine Ozeray. The exiles reassemble the old firm in a suburb of another country and make one picture with it. Then Lang takes the MGM contract and the firm scatters west, and Liliom stands alone in the filmography, in a language he made nothing else in.
suggested_refs: The Joinville studios, base of Erich Pommer's Fox-Europa from 1933

stops.name: New York, the French Line pier
stops.date_confidence: Arrival dated June 1934 by the geography record; the day is not established. [R] as to the berth: the pier number for the crossing is not confirmed, and the pin marks the Manhattan transatlantic piers. The chronology lens of this dossier dated the move to 1936 by folding it together with the release of Fury, and is corrected here.
stops.campa: He lands in New York contracted to MGM through David O. Selznick and goes on west. Ten years earlier he had come to this water as a visitor and taken a city home in his head; six years earlier he had told an English reporter he would never live in America because American editors had butchered Metropolis. Einstein has already wintered three years at Caltech and settled at Princeton the previous November. The exile traffic is running, and Lang is on it with a studio contract in his pocket.
stops.quote: I love films, so I shall never go to America. Their experts have slashed my best film, Metropolis, so cruelly that I dare not see it while I am in England.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang, press statement during a visit to Britain before he settled in the United States, quoted in Wikipedia's article on Metropolis (1927 film)
suggested_refs: The Manhattan French Line piers, terminus of the 1934 crossing

stops.name: Culver City, the MGM lot: Fury
stops.date_confidence: Fury is released on 5 June 1936; shooting runs through 1935 into 1936. Coordinates corrected to the MGM lot at 10202 West Washington Boulevard, now Sony Pictures Studios; an earlier atlas pin at 34.0247, -118.3892 sits about 1.3 kilometres northeast of the lot.
stops.campa: His first American film is about a mob: an innocent man taken for a kidnapper, a jail burned by a town, and the survivor who lets the town believe it killed him so that he can watch it tried. Spencer Tracy plays him. Lang has been in the country under two years and makes, first thing, a picture about ordinary people turning into a crowd and a crowd turning into a fire. MGM markets it as a thriller. It is the same subject as the cellar trial in M, moved to a country with no ruins yet.
suggested_refs: Fury (1936), Lang's first American production

stops.name: Hollywood, the United Artists lot: You Only Live Once
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. The lot pin is approximate and no stage address is confirmed in reachable sources.
stops.campa: A three-time loser and the woman who marries him run for a border they will not reach. The film gives American cinema a shape it keeps: the doomed couple in a stolen car, the law closing like weather. The next year he makes You and Me, and after that the studios begin to think of him as difficult and expensive, which he is. In these pictures the courts and the police work exactly as designed. They close on the wrong man, and nothing in the machinery has failed when they do.
suggested_refs: You Only Live Once (1937), a source text for American film noir

stops.name: Los Angeles, the federal courthouse: citizenship
stops.date_confidence: Naturalization attested for 1939 by both English and German Wikipedia; month and day are not established and default to 01. An earlier geography entry in this dossier gave 1935 and contradicted its own chronology; 1939 is followed. The courthouse building is not specified in reachable sources and the pin is an approximation for downtown Los Angeles.
stops.campa: The conscript of the Austro-Hungarian Landsturm becomes a citizen of the United States. He has been in the country five years and has made four pictures in its language. From here the passport that was his evidence against himself in 1933 stops mattering; he is an American director with a German accent and a monocle, which in the war years about to open will be a costume as much as a fact. Five years earlier the same government had let him in on a studio's word.
suggested_refs: Lang's US naturalization record, 1939

stops.name: Tuolumne County, the Sierra Railroad: The Return of Frank James
stops.date_confidence: The railroad scenes are documented on the Sierra Railroad in Tuolumne County, California; the pin marks the line's Jamestown depot as a regional anchor, not a documented setup, and the month is approximate. An earlier atlas stop put this film and Western Union together at Sedona, Arizona, 34.8697, -111.7610; Western Union was in fact shot at Fredonia, Arizona, and in southern Utah at Johnson Canyon, Paria, The Gap and Alton, plus the Fox lot, roughly 230 kilometres from Sedona. The Sedona pin is dropped.
stops.campa: The Viennese takes the western, in colour, on an American shortline railroad in the Sierra foothills: Jesse James's brother hunting the men who shot him in the back. The next year he makes Western Union in the red country of northern Arizona and southern Utah, and then Man Hunt, an Englishman stalking Hitler through a rifle scope and then stalked back across England. Twelve months carry him from the national frontier myth to the war, and the same camera serves both.
suggested_refs: The Sierra Railroad at Jamestown, California, filming location for The Return of Frank James
sources: English Wikipedia, 'The Return of Frank James'

stops.name: Hollywood, Hangmen Also Die! with Brecht
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. The production pin is approximate for the Hollywood studio district.
stops.campa: He writes with Bertolt Brecht, another Berlin exile in the sun, a fictional account of the killing of Reinhard Heydrich in Prague and of the hostages shot for it. Three years earlier the ministry that offered Lang the German industry had commissioned Veit Harlan to turn the eighteenth-century court Jew Joseph Oppenheimer into propaganda. The same office, the same minister: one film made for the Reich out of a dead man's story, one made against it out of a dead man's story, four thousand miles apart.
suggested_refs: Hangmen Also Die! (1943), the Lang and Brecht collaboration

stops.name: Beverly Hills, the noir years
stops.date_confidence: Period stop covering 1944 to 1956, dated at its middle with month and day defaulted to 01. The exact residence address is not established in reachable sources and the pin marks the district associated with Lang's Hollywood home.
stops.campa: Ministry of Fear and The Woman in the Window in 1944, Scarlet Street in 1945 with Edward G. Robinson and Joan Bennett, The Blue Gardenia and The Big Heat in 1953, and in 1956 While the City Sleeps and Beyond a Reasonable Doubt, the last films he makes in America. Twelve years of respectable men destroyed by one decision and of cities that work exactly as designed. He is in his sixties, the accent has not gone, and the country that took him in he films as a trap with good lighting.
suggested_refs: Scarlet Street (1945) and The Big Heat (1953), the American noir sequence

stops.name: Berlin-Haselhorst, CCC-Filmkunst
stops.date_confidence: Coordinates corrected to Verlaengerte Daumstrasse 16, Berlin-Haselhorst; an earlier atlas pin at 52.5390, 13.1930 falls about 1.8 kilometres west of the studio. The date marks the start of Artur Brauner's production run with Lang, 1958 to 1960; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The producer Artur Brauner brings him back to Germany after twenty-four years, to a studio in a Berlin suburb in a country divided down the middle. The commission is an old one: the two-part Indian adventure he and Thea von Harbou had wanted to make in the twenties, when Ufa gave the job to somebody else. He is sixty-seven and takes it. Whatever he refused in the corridor on the Wilhelmstrasse, he does not refuse a German studio once the men who ran the corridor are dead.
suggested_refs: CCC-Filmkunst, Verlaengerte Daumstrasse 16, Berlin-Haselhorst

stops.name: Udaipur, the City Palace and Lake Pichola
stops.date_confidence: Location work in Rajasthan is attested for the Indian Epic; some sources add forts of the Jaipur area, not independently confirmed here. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He shoots exteriors in Rajasthan for Der Tiger von Eschnapur and Das indische Grabmal: a palace on a lake, a temple dance, a maharajah's tomb. It is the only production of his life filmed on location in Asia, by the man who built a forest out of concrete rather than go to one. The critics who have canonised M and Metropolis find the Indian films gaudy and say so at length. The young men writing in Paris do not, and they are the ones about to reclaim the whole filmography.
suggested_refs: The City Palace and Lake Pichola, Udaipur, exteriors of the Indian Epic

stops.name: Berlin, Die 1000 Augen des Dr. Mabuse
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin repeats the CCC studio.
stops.campa: The third Mabuse, thirty-eight years after the first: a hotel wired with cameras and one-way glass, built by the Gestapo and inherited by a new criminal, everyone watched from everywhere. His sight is going as he shoots it and this is the last film he makes. Asked on the set what he is, he tells an actor he is not an artist, and then, so it stays said, that he is a craftsman. He has forty more years of reputation coming and sixteen more years of life, and he directs nothing in either.
stops.quote: I am not an artist. I am a craftsman.
stops.quote_source: Fritz Lang on the set of The 1,000 Eyes of Dr. Mabuse, 1960, reported in the Directors Guild of America Quarterly, Spring 2012; spoken to an actor as two statements rather than as one epigram
suggested_refs: Die 1000 Augen des Dr. Mabuse (1960), Lang's last film
sources: Directors Guild of America Quarterly, Spring 2012

segments.name: The Old Man in Beverly Hills

stops.name: Hollywood, 1600 Vine Street: the star
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 8 February 1960.
stops.campa: A brass star is set into the pavement at 1600 Vine Street for services to the motion picture industry, in the same season he is finishing the last Mabuse in a Berlin suburb. The industry that took twenty-two years of his working life gives him a paving stone the year he stops working. He will outlive the ceremony by sixteen years and be photographed on it by visitors who have come to ask him about Metropolis, which lost its money in 1927 and has not stopped earning since.
suggested_refs: Lang's star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, 1600 Vine Street

stops.name: Cannes, president of the jury
stops.date_confidence: Lang presides over the Cannes jury in 1964; the festival runs in May and the day is defaulted to 01. His appearance as himself in Godard's Contempt, an Italian and French production of 1963, is folded into this stop: the pool records no location for that film beyond the countries of production, so no separate pin is claimed for it.
stops.campa: The year before, Jean-Luc Godard put him in Contempt playing Fritz Lang, an old German director on a Mediterranean production being told by a producer what the Odyssey ought to mean. He plays himself with the monocle in. Now he sits at the head of the Cannes jury, judging the young men who canonised him while Hollywood was letting his contracts lapse. The films are behind him; the reputation, run entirely by French critics half his age, is only starting.
suggested_refs: Le Mepris (1963), in which Lang appears as himself

stops.name: Beverly Hills, the last house
stops.date_confidence: Death attested for 2 August 1976, of a stroke, at the age of 85. The marriage to Lily Latte is attested for 1971 in the United States, with no place or month given in reachable sources, and is folded into this stop. The address of the residence at death is not established.
stops.campa: He marries Lily Latte in 1971 and dies of a stroke on the second of August 1976, eighty-five years old, nearly blind, having made no film for sixteen years. The obituaries call him the man who made Metropolis and M, which is what the obituaries of 1976 have to work with; the twenty-two American pictures are a second paragraph. Godard's picture is thirteen years old, and for a younger audience his face is the one in it: an old man in a monocle explaining Homer to a producer. In the Vienna he was born in, nobody has yet put up a plaque, and when they do it will carry the wrong dates.
suggested_refs: Obituaries of Fritz Lang, August 1976

segments.name: Afterlife: the Reels in Buenos Aires

stops.name: Los Angeles, Forest Lawn Hollywood Hills: the grave
stops.date_confidence: Interment at Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills, attested for 1976; the day is not given in reachable sources and is set to the date of death rather than defaulted backwards. Coordinates corrected to 6300 Forest Lawn Drive, 34.145, -118.320; an earlier atlas pin at 34.1252, -118.3084 falls inside Griffith Park, about 2.5 kilometres southeast of the cemetery.
stops.campa: He is buried on Forest Lawn Drive in the Hollywood Hills, in the cemetery the industry uses, four thousand miles from the Schottenkirche and about the same from the hangar at Staaken. No monument, no epitaph reported in the sources reached. The estate and the reputation pass to Lily Latte and to the archives, and the correcting of his biography begins almost at once, because a man who told his own life as a screenplay leaves an unusual amount of work for the people who come after.
suggested_refs: Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills, 6300 Forest Lawn Drive
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills'

stops.name: Vienna, Zeltgasse 1: the plaque with the wrong dates
stops.date_confidence: The plaque is installed in 1979 at Zeltgasse 1 in the eighth district, Josefstadt, the corner building whose three frontages give the address three street names, Zeltgasse, Piaristengasse and Neudeggergasse; no month is given, so it defaults to 01. The coordinates fall within about 200 metres of the building. This is a later family residence and not the birth address at Schenkenstrasse 6.
stops.campa: Three years after his death Vienna fixes a memorial tablet to a corner house in the Josefstadt where the Langs had lived, a building with three street names and one plaque. In 1986 the film scholar Cornelius Schnauber points out that the dates cut into it are wrong. The city has commemorated a man who spent sixty years giving out incorrect dates about himself, and has got the dates incorrect. The tablet is not corrected. It marks the wrong house for the birth as well.
stops.quote: Die Fritz-Lang-Gedenktafel am Wohnhaus in der Piaristengasse in Wien enthaelt leider falsche Daten.
stops.quote_source: Cornelius Schnauber, 1986, cited in German Wikipedia, 'Fritz Lang'; umlauts transliterated
suggested_refs: The 1979 Fritz Lang Gedenktafel at Zeltgasse 1, Vienna 8
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Fritz Lang', citing Cornelius Schnauber (1986)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Museo del Cine: the missing reels
stops.date_confidence: Announcement attested for 1 July 2008: a 16mm safety reduction negative holding about twenty-five minutes of the 1927 cut unseen since the premiere, traced by Fernando Martin Pena and identified with the museum's director Paula Felix-Didier. Coordinates are the Museo del Cine Pablo Ducros Hicken at its La Boca building; the museum moved there only on 1 August 2011, and its 2008 premises are not identified in reachable sources. An earlier atlas pin at -34.6118, -58.4120 is about 5.5 kilometres off. The corpus pin for Buenos Aires, from Falconetti's journey, is -34.6037, -58.3816.
stops.campa: A film historian in Buenos Aires hears an anecdote about a copy of Metropolis that runs too long, and follows it for years into a museum archive: a 16mm reduction negative with twenty-five minutes nobody has seen since January 1927. The city that kept Falconetti through her exile and buried her in 1946 has been holding Lang's missing reels in a can. Whatever Europe burns or cuts, some print of it ends up at the far end of the Atlantic, filed under the wrong length and waiting.
suggested_refs: The Museo del Cine Pablo Ducros Hicken and the 2008 Metropolis reduction negative

stops.name: Berlin, the Friedrichstadtpalast: Metropolis restored
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 12 February 2010, simultaneous with an open-air screening at the Brandenburg Gate and a showing at the Alte Oper in Frankfurt; the North American premiere follows on 25 April 2010 at Mann's Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles.
stops.campa: Eighty-three years after the Ufa-Palast, the Buenos Aires footage is married to the Murnau-Stiftung restoration and Metropolis opens again in Berlin: the Friedrichstadtpalast, the Brandenburg Gate in the open air with an orchestra, the Alte Oper in Frankfurt, all in one night. The film that lost Ufa its independence and was cut to pieces on both sides of the Atlantic is shown nearly whole to a city that no longer has a wall in it. Lang has been dead thirty-four years and is still in the release schedule.
stops.quote: Without Fritz, there'd be no Star Wars.
stops.quote_source: Philip French, The Observer, as reproduced in the Wikipedia article on Lang; a judgement about Lang, not by him
suggested_refs: The 2010 restored Metropolis, Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung
